mcqs.question: In the LCS recurrence, what happens at dp[i][j] when A[i-1] equals B[j-1]?
options: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 — the matching characters extend a shared subsequence diagonally
dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]), the same as a mismatch
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1], with no increment
dp[i][j] = 0, resetting because a match was found
mcqs.explanation: A matching pair of characters can both be included in a common subsequence, so the length grows by exactly one over the best answer using both strings' prefixes one character shorter — the diagonal cell. Taking the max of the neighbors is only for the mismatch case.

mcqs.question: Edit Distance's dp[i][j] has three candidate values every time, unlike LCS's two. Why does Edit Distance always need all three?
options: Because Edit Distance requires the two strings to be the same length
Because Edit Distance uses a different table shape than LCS
Because the base cases require three separate arrays
Because insert, delete, and replace are three genuinely different operations, and even a matching character still has a cost-0 replace option competing with insert and delete
mcqs.explanation: Every cell maps to three real edit operations — delete from A, insert to match B, or replace/keep — so all three are always live candidates, even on a character match, where the diagonal 'replace' move simply costs 0 instead of 1. LCS only had two live neighbors because a mismatch there has no diagonal option at all.

mcqs.question: LCS and Edit Distance use the same grid shape and the same off-by-one handling. What's the core difference between them?
options: LCS optimizes for keeping (matching) characters via max; Edit Distance prices changing characters via min over three operations
LCS requires sorting the strings first; Edit Distance does not
Edit Distance only works on strings of equal length; LCS works on any lengths
LCS is O(n+m); Edit Distance is O(n·m)
mcqs.explanation: Both use dp[i][j] over two prefix-length axes with the same empty-prefix base row/column, but LCS asks 'how much can I keep in common' (maximize matches), while Edit Distance asks 'what's the cheapest way to transform one into the other' (minimize operation cost) — same skeleton, opposite objective and neighbor count.

mcqs.question: The LCS table is sized (n+1) x (m+1) rather than n x m. Why?
options: To leave room for a sentinel value used during binary search
So row 0 and column 0 can represent 'zero characters consumed from that string,' making the diagonal and neighbor lookups valid even at the first real character
Because the strings are 1-indexed in most languages
It's an arbitrary convention with no functional purpose
mcqs.explanation: The extra row and column are the empty-prefix base cases — without them, the very first real comparison at i=1, j=1 would have no valid dp[0][0] to reference. The characters themselves are still accessed with a -1 offset (A[i-1], B[j-1]) inside the loop.

mcqs.question: A problem asks for the longest common substring instead of longest common subsequence. Can you reuse the LCS recurrence unchanged?
options: Yes, substring and subsequence are interchangeable terms for this problem
Yes, but only the base row and column need to change
No — substring requires contiguity, so on a mismatch the recurrence must reset to 0 instead of taking the max of neighboring cells
No — substring problems can't be solved with any 2D DP table
mcqs.explanation: A subsequence can skip characters freely; a substring cannot have gaps, so a mismatch breaks any run in progress and the recurrence must reset to 0 rather than carrying forward the best neighboring value. Treating the two as the same problem produces a recurrence that solves the wrong question.
